title: Pyramid Texts of Unas: Utterances 247-253 (antechamber, west gable)
source: Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara, antechamber, west gable (photograph: L. F. Husson for A. Piankoff 1968, via Pyramid Texts Online) + TLA transliteration (ed. D. Topmann, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of S. A. B. Mercer (1952, public domain in the US)
description: The Pyramid Texts on the west gable of the antechamber in the pyramid of Unas (c. 2350 BCE), utterance by utterance, with the TLA transliteration and Mercer's English.
introduction:
The Pyramid Texts are the oldest large body of Egyptian religious writing: spells, called utterances, for the resurrection of the dead king, his protection, his meals and his ascent to the sky, cut in vertical columns of hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial apartments of late Old Kingdom pyramids. The pyramid of Unas at Saqqara, the last king of the 5th Dynasty (about 2375-2345 BCE), is the first to carry them. Its sarcophagus chamber, the passage to the antechamber, the antechamber and the corridor hold 649 numbered columns of text; this library gives every column, wall by wall, in seventeen entries (227 different utterances, some of them inscribed more than once).

This entry is the west gable of the antechamber: 37 columns of hieroglyphs, Sethe's W 379-415, which follow each other from the right-hand (north) edge of the photograph. It holds the utterances 247, 248, 249, 250, 251, 252, 253.

Each section is one utterance. The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Doris Topmann), with Sethe's Unas column number (W) before each column; a number ending in 'a' marks the offering label at the foot of a column. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, damaged signs in half brackets. The English is Samuel A. B. Mercer's translation of 1952. Mercer translates Sethe's composite text made from all the pyramids that have an utterance, so his wording can include clauses that are not in the Unas copy, and his section numbers (134a, 134b ...) are Sethe's paragraph numbers, not column numbers; he writes 'N.' where the wall has the king's name. The photograph shows the whole wall; each section's note gives its columns counted from the edge where the text on that wall begins.
translator_notes: Mercer's separate headings, postscripts and variants taken from other pyramids are left out.
Letters follow the sacred-texts transcription of Mercer: ȝ stands for aleph and ‘ for ayin; letters underlined in the printed book are given as ḏ, ṯ, ẖ.
Sethe's section numbers are kept as printed in that transcription, including a few misprints (for example '146.' for 141b in Utterance 215).
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

translation.text:
257aTo say: Thy son Horus has done (this) for thee.
257bThe great tremble when they have seen the sword which is in thy hand,
257cas thou comest forth from the Dwȝ-t.
258aGreetings to thee, wise one.
258bGeb has created thee; the Ennead have engendered thee.
258cHorus is satisfied with his father, (as) Atum is satisfied with his years.
258dThe gods of the East and West are satisfied with the great (thing) which is come to pass in the embrace of the divine mother (Nut).
259aN., O. N., (thou) who hast seen; N., O. N., (thou) who hast regarded;
259bN, O (thou) who hast heard; N., O N., (thou) who hast been there;
260aN., O N., lift thee up upon thy side, (thou) doer of command;
260b(thou) who hatest sleep, (thou) who art made tired, stand up, (thou) who art in Ndi.t.
260cThy fine bread is made (i.e. offered, cf. CT, I Spell 67, 286b) in Buto; take thy power in Heliopolis.
261aThis Horus commanded to do (this) for his father. The lord of tempest prevented the saliva of Set,
261bwhen he (Set) should carry thee. It is he who will carry the one who is (again) complete.

262aTo say; N. is great. N. has come forth from between the thighs of the Ennead.
262bN. was, conceived by Sekhmet, it is Šsmt.t who gave birth to N.,
263a(as) the star with piercing front (glance) and wide of stride, who brings provisions for (his) journey to Rē‘ every day.
263bN. has come to his throne, which is higher than (or, over, above) the two protective goddesses of Upper and Lower Egypt; N. appears (or, shines) as a star.

264aTo say: O ye two contestants, announce now to the honourable one in this his name:
264bN. is this sšsš-plant which springs from the earth.
264cThe hand of N. is cleansed by him who has prepared his throne.
265aN. it is who is at the nose of the powerful Great One.
265bN. comes out of the Isle of Flame,
265c(after) he, N., had set truth therein in the place of error.
265dN. it is who is the guardian of laundry, who protects the uraeus-serpents,
265ein the night of the great flood, which proceeds from the Great.
266aN. appears as Nefertem, as the flower of the lotus at the nose of Rē‘;
266bas he comes forth from the horizon every day, the gods purify themselves, when they see him.

translation.text:
267aTo say: "It is N. who is chief of the kas, who unites the hearts," so says be (or she) who is chief of the wise, the Great One,
267b"he who is in possession of the divine book, who knows, who is at the right of Rē‘."
267cN. comes to his throne, he is chief of the kas, N. unites the hearts, (so says she) who is chief of the wise, the Great One,
267dN. comes into being, he who knows, being in possession of the divine book, he who is at the right of Rē‘.
268aO thou who art vindicated by N.,
268bit is N. who says (is saying) what is in the heart of the Great One (Nut), at the Feast of Red Clothes,
268c(for) it is N., it is N., who knows, who is at the right of Rē‘;
268d(thus) the heart of the chief of the abyss of Nun is vexed.

translation.text:
269aTo say: O ye, who are (set) over the hours, who are (go) before Rē‘, make (ready) the way for N.,
269bthat N. may pass through in the midst of the border guard of hostile mien.
270aN. is on the way to his throne, (like) one whose places are in front, who is behind the god, with bowed head,
270badorned with a sharp (and) strong antelope's horn,
270clike one in possession of a sharp knife, which cuts the throat.
270dThe driver-away (?) of suffering from the bull, the punisher of those in darkness,
270e(is) the strong antelope's horn, which is behind the Great God.
271aN. has reduced them to punishment; N. has crushed their head.
271bThe arm of N. will not be resisted in the horizon.

272aTo say: Lift up your head, ye gods, who are in the Dwȝ.t,
272bfor N. is come. Ye see him (how) he becomes as, a great god.
272cIntroduce N. with trembling; adorn N.,
273awho has honoured ye all, (as) he commanded mankind (also to do).
273bN. judges those who live in the midst of the land of Rē‘,
273cas N. speaks to this pure land, wherein he has established his residence, with the judge of the two gods,
274aN. is mighty in his presence; N. bears the ȝmś-sceptre, when he (Thot) would reject N.
274bN. sits with those who row Rē‘.
274cN. commands the good, and he (Thot) does it, (for) N. is the Great God.

275aTo say: He is pure, who was purified in the Marsh of Reeds.
275bRē‘ is purified in the Marsh of Reeds.
275cHe is pure, who was purified in the Marsh of Reeds.
275dThis N. is purified in the Marsh of Reeds.
275eThe hand of N. is in the hand of Rē‘; Nut takes his arm;
275fShu lifts him up; Shu lifts him up.
